title: Why Rethink Hell?
hook: Can God offer infinite mercy and enforce infinite torture at the same time?
tldr: The Augustinian-Calvinist 'Hellfire' view says God torments most of humanity forever. It contradicts God's mercy and harms mental health. Two thousand years of Roman, Greek, European and American reshaping, biased translations and anachronism have buried the Bible's Jewish context. The goal is to read these Jewish texts as their first audience did.
big_idea: Read the Bible in its own Jewish context, not through later creeds.

points.title: The 'Good News' as a threat
points.text: The opening joke: Jesus knocks, offering to save you from what He will do to you if you don't open. For some, that is the gospel.

points.title: Hell versus Hellfire
points.text: 'Hell' covers many views, from literal fire to metaphor, eternal damnation to temporary purification. 'Hellfire' means only the Augustinian-Calvinist Eternal Conscious Torment view.

points.title: Mercy and torture contradict
points.text: You cannot preach infinite mercy and enforce infinite torture. Mercy with an expiration date is leverage: love with a gun to your head. God reconciles all things to Himself.

points.title: Doctrine affects mental health
points.text: Harsh views of hell breed anxiety, depression, fear and harsh judgment of others. A compassionate, logical view can free people from existential fear and legalism.

points.title: Lost in translation and time
points.text: Hebrew's three-consonant roots resist translation, translators' theology shapes word choices, and the Anachronism Fallacy projects modern ideas onto ancient texts.

points.title: Back to the original context
points.text: The goal: move past 2,000 years of Western, non-Jewish readings and understand these Jewish texts as their original, mostly Jewish audience would.

sections.summary: Starting a serious topic with a joke: Jesus knocks and says, open up so I can save you. Save me from what? 'From what I am going to do to you if you don't open!' That is the 'Good News' according to some. If it shocked you, good: the book aims for the opposite effect.

'Hell' is a broad doctrine with diverse readings: a literal place of fire or a symbolic metaphor, eternal damnation or a temporary process of purification. 'Hellfire' specifically means the Augustinian-Calvinist depiction of a literal place of endless torture in fire, the ECT (Eternal Conscious Torment) view. The chapters have a logical flow and are best read in order.

The shorter book mostly combines 'Hell in the Bible' from 'HELL: A Jewish Perspective on a Christian Doctrine' and 'Rethinking Hell' from 'The Gospel Before Christianity', with original thoughts, so some overlap and repetition occurs.

sections.h: Preface: love with a gun to your head
sections.summary: Everyone wants to feel safe, avoid pain and believe it will be okay; Christianity offered a merciful, protective Father. Then came ECT: God keeping people alive in fire forever with no exit, healing, hope or end. Beyond cruelty, it is a contradiction: mercy with an expiration date is leverage. Remove ECT and God looks like God; keep it and He offers love with a gun to your head.

Scholar Michael S. Heiser: the proper context for the Bible is not Augustine, the Catholic Church, rabbinic movements, the Reformation, the Puritans or evangelicalism, but the biblical writers' own context. As a Jewish believer in Jesus, the author sees Jews and Christians reading differently on hell, sin, atonement, salvation and divorce.

sections.h: The Hellfire view and mental health
sections.summary: Some conservative Protestants, Baptist, Calvinist, Lutheran, Pentecostal, Evangelical and other fundamentalists, hold that God eternally torments billions, some say by burning, every minute forever. Such views can cause anxiety, depression, fear and harsh judgment of others. Critics call Hellfire illogical and a misrepresentation of a God of love, mercy and corrective justice; a compassionate view can heal faith-life.

Christianity drifted far from its Jewish roots over two thousand years: adapted to Rome's anti-Jewish sentiment and Greek philosophy, recontextualized for European pagans, altered in the Reformation wars, then adapted to America's settlement. Traces of the original Gospel remain, mixed with traditions, biases, mistranslations and cultural accretions. The Bible, ancient Jewish documents full of metaphor, parable and allegory, confuses Westerners unfamiliar with its world.

Language evolves, and Hebrew and Greek words carry a spectrum of meanings only context clarifies. Hebrew and Aramaic build words from three-consonant roots, with vowel patterns adding grammar, unlike English prefixes and suffixes. The Genesis 3 'serpent', nachash, can also mean copper, shining or bronze; Jewish tradition (Bereshit Rabbah 20:5) sees a shining being, like Paul's Satan as 'an angel of light'.

Translation choices reflect translators' theology, perhaps why over 900 English Bibles exist. In Matthew 10:29 the Greek has no word for knowledge or will. The NAB says 'without your Father's knowledge'; the KJV, literally, 'without your Father'. The NET, by a Calvinist group, adds 'will', fitting TULIP predestination where everything happens because God wills it, negating free will.

For a Jewish reader who lost family in the Holocaust, the NET's addition is troubling: it suggests Jesus taught that God actively willed such atrocities, making Him seem indifferent to suffering and endorsing evil as divinely ordained. For Jews with a history of loss, this is theologically revolting and alienating. In Judaism, free will, God's mercy and compassion are core tenets.

The Anachronism Fallacy places ideas, concepts or customs in a period where they do not belong, like reading today's meaning of 'gay' into a century-old book. It is common in modern teaching on the 'hell' verses. Worse, 45,000 (elsewhere 49,000) Christian groups each believe only they read the Bible right, a conviction that fueled violent conflicts over salvation, faith and hell.

The aim is to transcend over 2,000 years of Western, non-Jewish interpretation and read these Jewish texts as their mostly Jewish audience would, studying historical context, ancient word usage and later translation choices, without modern bias. Written simply by a native Hebrew speaker from Israel who studied Greek in seminary, it offers no yes-or-no answers, only challenges to sacrosanct assumptions and new perspectives.

The full book has four parts. Part I surveys how the concept of hell evolved. Part II examines the doctrines underpinning Augustinian-Calvinist Hellfire. Part III scrutinizes key passages and terms tied to hell. Part IV offers reflections on God's justice, salvation and hell. A Jewish perspective runs throughout, illuminating where some Christian teachings deviate.

mythfact.myth: Our English Bibles say exactly what the original text says.
mythfact.fact: Translators' theology shapes choices. The NET adds 'will' to Matthew 10:29, a word absent from the Greek.

mythfact.myth: Hell and Hellfire mean the same thing.
mythfact.fact: Hell covers many views. Hellfire is the specific Augustinian-Calvinist view of eternal conscious torment in literal fire.

mythfact.myth: What you believe about hell doesn't affect your wellbeing.
mythfact.fact: Harsh views can produce anxiety, depression, fear and harsh judgment; a compassionate view can foster healthier spiritual life.

quiz.q: What does 'Hellfire' specifically mean in these books?
options: The Augustinian-Calvinist Eternal Conscious Torment view
quiz.why: Hell is the broad term; Hellfire names only the view of a literal place of endless torture in fire.

quiz.q: What did the NET translation add to Matthew 10:29?
quiz.why: The Greek has no such word; 'will' fits Calvinist predestination, implying God willed every death.

quiz.q: Reading today's meaning of 'gay' into a century-old book illustrates what?
quiz.why: It projects modern meanings onto past texts, a fallacy common in modern teaching on hell verses.
